questions.q: What isolation level does a new SQL Server connection run under by default, with no SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL statement at all?
options: READ COMMITTED
READ UNCOMMITTED
REPEATABLE READ
SERIALIZABLE
questions.explain: READ COMMITTED is SQL Server's default isolation level for every new session unless something else is explicitly set.

questions.q: What does READ COMMITTED guarantee that READ UNCOMMITTED does not?
options: Every read sees a consistent snapshot of the whole database
No blocking ever occurs under any circumstance
Every read only ever sees committed data -- dirty reads are prevented
Phantom reads are prevented
questions.explain: READ COMMITTED's one core guarantee is that reads never see another transaction's uncommitted, in-flight changes.

questions.q: Why does READ COMMITTED still allow nonrepeatable reads and phantom reads?
options: It only holds its shared locks for the duration of each individual statement's read, not for the whole transaction
It doesn't take any locks at all, same as READ UNCOMMITTED
It holds locks for the whole transaction, but ignores updates from other sessions
It only applies to INSERT and DELETE statements, not SELECT
questions.explain: Because the lock is released as soon as a statement's read finishes, another transaction can commit a change (or insert/delete a matching row) before a second read in the same transaction runs.

questions.q: In the dirty-read timeline from Lesson 92, what would happen differently if Session B ran under READ COMMITTED instead of READ UNCOMMITTED?
options: Session B would still read the dirty, uncommitted value immediately
Session B's read would block, waiting for Session A's lock to release via commit or rollback, instead of reading the uncommitted value
Nothing would change -- READ COMMITTED behaves identically to READ UNCOMMITTED
Session A's transaction would fail instead
questions.explain: READ COMMITTED requires reads to only see committed data, so it would wait rather than read Session A's in-flight 9999.00 value.

questions.q: What command lets you confirm which isolation level the current session is actually running under?
options: SELECT @@ISOLATION;
SHOW TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL;
EXEC sp_isolation_level;
DBCC USEROPTIONS;
questions.explain: DBCC USEROPTIONS returns a result set that includes an 'isolation level' row showing the current session's active setting.
